body: The keys to the building are on the passenger seat and the woman they belong to is still behind the wheel, engine off, in a church car park at twenty to nine on a Sunday. There is a box of teabags and long-life milk in the boot, because she has done the coffee since her eldest was in primary school and her eldest is twenty-six. Nothing is wrong. Nobody has hurt her, she is not angry with God, and she is not entertaining a doubt she could put into a sentence. She has been sitting there for eleven minutes. In a moment she will pick up the keys, go in, and put the urn on.
Nothing happened in that car park, and that is exactly what makes it impossible to talk about. There is no event. There is nobody to forgive and nothing to renounce. There is not even a question.

The assumption built into the phrase when faith feels hard is that difficulty belongs to the beginning — that it is hard while it is new, and then it settles. It is a comforting model. It does not match a great many actual lives.

It is worth being precise, because the two are not the same trouble. The beginner has difficulty because everything is friction: the language is strange, the practices are awkward, and belief keeps running into a life that was built without it. That difficulty is loud and it has edges you can push against. What arrives at year twenty has no edges at all. The practices still run — she will pray at the urn, and mean it. The friction is gone and so is everything else. It is not disproof, which could be argued with. It is silence, in a person who has organised her entire week around expecting to be spoken to, and there is no obvious way to bring that up in a room where the correct answer is that God is good.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. The hard stretches are not treated as one mood handled by one station. They are spread across several, at real frequencies, with schedules.

Programming for this listener costs a station its easiest audience. The long-serving are not a growth market. They are already committed, they will not be converted, and they rarely write in. Worse, saying the thing out loud frightens the new — nobody wants to hear, in year one, what year twenty can be like. But somebody has to say it, because nobody warns you that the hardest stretch tends to arrive in year twenty, to someone doing everything right, and the not-warning is a large part of the damage.

The silence is not a modern complaint. It runs through the middle of most of the psalms, where the singer is not a sceptic but a man who has been faithful for years and cannot find God in the room. It is the whole of Ecclesiastes, a long life of doing the right things and finding it thin. It is Elijah under the juniper tree, asking to die, three days after the greatest public vindication of his career. Collapse-after-triumph is in the text because it is in people.

Church culture is embarrassed by it. The testimony has a shape: I was lost, then this happened, now I am found. It is a true shape and it is the wrong length. There is no slot in it for twenty years in and gone quiet, so people in that condition learn that the honest answer makes the room uncomfortable, and they say fine instead. Then each of them concludes, privately, that they are the only one — which is what a car park at twenty to nine is actually made of.
So the question is not what to say to such a person. It is what should be playing.

The obvious answer is encouragement, and it is not a stupid answer. A station of relentless uplift is kindly meant, and on an ordinary bad Tuesday it works: a person can be carried by three minutes of somebody insisting that God is faithful. But it assumes the problem is a deficit of morale, and hers is not. She believes God is faithful; she has believed it through two funerals and a redundancy. Being told energetically what you already hold, by a voice that has plainly never been where you are, is not company. It is instruction, delivered at volume, and it produces a very specific loneliness: you feel unmet in the middle of being encouraged, and you cannot say so without sounding ungrateful.
You cannot be encouraged out of year twenty. You can only be accompanied through it.

A man of sixty-one wakes at ten past three and works out how long it is until it would be reasonable to get up. He stopped praying in bed about two years ago — not by any decision, but because he ran out of sentences and got tired of hearing himself start the same one. So he goes down in his dressing gown, fills the kettle, and puts something on low over the counter so the house has a sound in it. He does not sing. He does not pray, exactly. He sits at the end of the table with a mug and lets the room be occupied by something other than himself until the sky starts, and then goes back up and sleeps for an hour and a half. He has done this, on and off, for two years, and has told nobody.

That is not a crisis and it will never be a testimony. It is what faithfulness looks like in the flat years, and the only thing keeping it company is something that does not require him to feel anything to let him in.

The honest cost of a station that takes this seriously is that it will not lift you, and some nights you will want lifting. There are evenings when what a person needs is a shout, and a frequency built for the long quiet will hand them a slow one instead. It cannot fix anything either. The silence does not end because of a radio station. Twenty years in, a person can tell the difference between company and a promise of results, and they have stopped believing the second one.

But that refusal to lift is the whole of the offer. A station that promised to raise him would have had to lie to him on the first night, and he would have switched it off inside a week — not out of cynicism, but because he can recognise a voice that is managing him. Something that simply keeps going in the room at three, making no claim about how he ought to feel by four, is the only thing he can leave running. Being accompanied without being addressed is what he can bear, and it turns out to be quite a lot.

So this is not a station for doubters or for newcomers. It is for the long-serving, in the flat years, who have nowhere to put it — and its one claim is that this stretch is an ordinary part of the road rather than a failure to be repaired. Year twenty is not the exception to the faith. It is most of it, and the people in it deserve music that knows that.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel and much else. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: clean, entertaining, and playable in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, 40 of them across 29 languages, hosted in their own tongues rather than translated into them afterwards.

If you are in that stretch, start at HM 313.80 — The Ancient Paths. Two reasons, both of them from the argument above. The first is the name, which comes from a prophet telling a people to stand in the ways and ask for the old paths: that instruction was never given to beginners, but to a nation a long way in that had lost the thread. The second is the music. It is Arabic and Middle Eastern worship — maqam-based, with a great deal of acoustic lament — and it comes out of a tradition that never assumed the singer was having a good day. Lament there is ordinary. It is not a special episode, or the pastoral exception to a general rule of brightness. It is simply part of how the week sounds, which is precisely the vocabulary the flat years lack.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen if you want it closer to hand. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people reach for at three in the morning — which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not go looking for the track that will finally shift something; that is the encouragement model, and you have tried it. Put HM 313.80 on low the next time you are up at an hour you did not choose, and then get on with the kettle. Let it be in the room without being addressed to you. That is the whole of what is being offered, and after twenty years you are probably the only sort of person who can tell how much it is worth.
